extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in entertainment, comedy, and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards about using race-related material in comedy, drawn from a news report of a comedian's controversial sketch and its professional fallout. Focuses on norms, audience perceptions, and likely consequences for racially charged humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donning blackface is never OK
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarah Silverman said she 'understood that wearing blackface is "never OK".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states this as a categorical moral standard. It notes blackface has a long history in American entertainment and is considered deeply racist and offensive to African Americans. Practitioners should avoid using blackface under any claimed satirical intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackface is deeply racist and offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: "Blackface, which has a long history in American entertainment, is considered deeply racist and offensive to African Americans."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames the historical and social harms associated with the practice: performers and creators should recognize the historical context and likely audience reaction before attempting race-related portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to critique does not absolve harmful methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Silverman put on blackface 'in an effort to prove a point about who faces more discrimination, Jews or African-Americans.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece illustrates that a stated critical or satirical intent (to prove a point about discrimination) may not prevent a sketch from being judged offensive by producers or audiences. Creators should not assume critical framing will protect them from reputational or professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racially charged routines can court controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes this is not Silverman’s first racially charged routine (e.g., dressing as Adolf Hitler on Conan in 2016) and that such acts 'have courted controversy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History of controversy signals that racially provocative material often provokes public backlash, debate, and media coverage. Comedians should weigh comedic goals against probable controversy and its impacts on career and public standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producers/employers may take immediate action when offensive material surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Silverman said she was fired from a movie role 'at 11 p.m. the night before' because producers saw a picture of her in blackface from an episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional consequences can be swift and decisive: employers may cancel roles or projects when they discover past or present material judged offensive. Performers should be aware that existing work or archival images can affect employment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedians may themselves be targets of harassment when involved in controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reports Silverman 'recently was subject to racial harassment herself' after tweeting a video of an anti-Semitic rant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy can lead to both public criticism and targeted harassment of the performer. Consider personal safety and mental-health implications when engaging in or publicizing contentious material.
